sentences: Many sports improve heart health.
Swimming strengthens the heart.
drills.hint: Use a semicolon before "for example" and a comma after it.

sentences: Some jobs can be done from home.
Software developers often work remotely.
drills.hint: Make the general point first, then give a specific example.

sentences: Some foods are high in hidden sugar.
Fruit yoghurt is one of them.
drills.hint: An example can go in the middle of a sentence, between two commas.

sentences: Cities can reduce congestion.
They can charge drivers to enter the centre.
drills.hint: The example shows one way to achieve the general idea in the first clause.

sentences: Technology has changed education.
Many lectures are now available online.
drills.hint: The second clause supports the first, so it is an example, not a contrast.

sentences: Some animals have adapted to city life.
Foxes now live in many urban areas.
answer: now live in many urban areas.
drills.hint: Put the general statement first; the linker introduces the specific case.

sentences: Many teenagers have part-time jobs.
Some work in shops at weekends.
drills.hint: "For instance" works like "for example": semicolon before, comma after.

sentences: Plastic waste harms sea life.
Turtles often swallow plastic bags.
drills.hint: The specific case follows the general problem.

sentences: Some diseases can be prevented by vaccines.
Measles is one of them.
drills.hint: Place the example between commas right after the noun it describes.

sentences: Many traditional crafts are disappearing.
Hand weaving is rarely taught today.
drills.hint: The second idea is one case of the first, so introduce it as an example.

sentences: Exercise can improve mood.
A short walk can reduce stress.
drills.hint: Use a comma after the linker before the example clause.

sentences: Some governments encourage cycling.
They offer tax breaks on new bicycles.
drills.hint: The example explains how the general policy works in practice.

sentences: Team sports teach cooperation.
Football and rugby are examples.
drills.hint: "Such as" comes straight after the noun it gives examples of.

sentences: Renewable sources are becoming cheaper.
Wind and solar power are examples.
drills.hint: "Such as" is followed by nouns, not a full clause.

sentences: Practical skills are hard to learn online.
Cooking and nursing are examples.
drills.hint: The examples go between the subject and its verb.

sentences: Older people often suffer from health conditions.
Arthritis and heart disease are common examples.
drills.hint: "Such as" + examples can end the sentence after the noun they describe.

sentences: Social media platforms spread news quickly.
Video-sharing apps are one example.
drills.hint: Keep the examples next to the general noun, before the main verb.

sentences: Simple habits can save energy.
Turning off lights is one such habit.
drills.hint: "Such as" can be followed by an -ing form; here commas surround the example.

sentences: Two subjects are compulsory.
They are maths and English.
drills.hint: "Namely" names exactly the things just mentioned; put a comma before it.

sentences: The city has one major problem.
This problem is air pollution.
drills.hint: Use "namely" to say exactly what the problem is.

sentences: The report identifies three causes of obesity.
These are diet, inactivity and stress.
drills.hint: After "namely", list all the items that were counted before it.

sentences: Only one group improved its scores.
This was the group of youngest students.
drills.hint: "Namely" identifies the exact group mentioned before the comma.

sentences: The firm is entering two new markets.
These are India and Brazil.
drills.hint: The number in the first part must match the items after "namely".

sentences: The plan has a clear aim.
It aims to cut emissions by half.
drills.hint: "Namely" can be followed by a to-infinitive that explains the aim.

sentences: Exercise benefits mental health.
Regular walkers report lower stress levels.
drills.hint: "To illustrate" introduces evidence for the point; it takes a comma.

sentences: Housing costs in the city have risen sharply.
A small flat now costs twice as much.
drills.hint: The second clause shows the size of the rise, so it illustrates the first.

sentences: Languages borrow words from each other.
English has taken many words from French.
drills.hint: Give the general claim, a semicolon, then the illustrating case.

sentences: Small changes can save a lot of water.
A shorter shower saves many litres.
answer: can save a lot of water;
drills.hint: The linker introduces a concrete case that supports the general point.

sentences: Air pollution harms many people.
Children are especially at risk.
drills.hint: "In particular" can follow the group it singles out, at the end.

sentences: Teenagers use many apps.
Video apps are very popular with them.
drills.hint: Here "in particular" sits between commas after the subject.

sentences: Several sectors face labour shortages.
Healthcare is badly affected.
drills.hint: Single out one sector by placing the phrase after it, between commas.

sentences: Tourism brings many benefits.
It creates jobs for young local people.
drills.hint: After a semicolon, "in particular" introduces the most important benefit.

sentences: The survey studied eating habits.
It focused on what people eat for breakfast.
drills.hint: "In particular" narrows a general topic to one specific part.

sentences: Many factors affect learning.
Sleep is especially vital.
drills.hint: Use commas around the phrase when it follows the subject it stresses.

sentences: Fast food is popular.
Teenagers like it most of all.
drills.hint: "Particularly" adds the group where the point is strongest.

sentences: Cycling has become popular.
This is most true in large cities.
drills.hint: A comma comes before "particularly" + the place phrase.

sentences: Older people benefit from gentle exercise.
Swimming is the most helpful.
drills.hint: Put the most important example after "particularly" at the end.

sentences: Water shortages are a growing problem.
They are most severe in dry regions.
drills.hint: "Particularly" stresses where the problem is worst.

sentences: The scheme helps students.
It mainly helps those from poor families.
drills.hint: Use "those" after "particularly" to refer back to the students.

sentences: Noise pollution affects health.
Its effect on sleep is especially serious.
drills.hint: "Particularly" can come before a "by" + -ing phrase showing the main effect.

sentences: Many tourists visit the coast.
Most of them come in summer.
drills.hint: "Especially" + time phrase shows when something is most true.

sentences: Online learning suits many adults.
It suits those with full-time jobs most.
drills.hint: Put a comma before "especially" when it adds a group at the end.

sentences: High housing costs are hard for many people.
Young families suffer the most.
drills.hint: "Especially" points to the group most affected.

sentences: Sugar harms people's teeth.
Young children's teeth are most at risk.
drills.hint: Use "especially" + a short phrase to show where the harm is greatest.

sentences: Recycling rates have risen.
The rate for glass has risen most.
drills.hint: "Especially" highlights the strongest case of a general trend.

sentences: Flexible working is valued by many staff.
Parents of young children value it most.
drills.hint: The phrase after "especially" must fit the passive "by many staff".

sentences: Many subjects are taught online.
Art and music are among them.
drills.hint: "Including" + examples can go between commas after the subject.

sentences: The museum has many exhibits.
Some ancient coins are among them.
drills.hint: "Including" is followed by a noun phrase, not a clause.

sentences: Several factors cause stress.
Long working hours are one factor.
drills.hint: Keep the example inside commas, then add the verb.

sentences: The festival attracts many visitors.
Families and students are among them.
drills.hint: Use a comma before "including" when it ends the sentence.

sentences: Diet affects many illnesses.
Diabetes is one of them.
drills.hint: "Including" shows the example is part of a bigger group.

sentences: The course covers several skills.
Writing an academic essay is one of them.
drills.hint: "Including" can be followed by a "how to" phrase.

sentences: The course is very demanding.
Many students drop out.
drills.hint: "Indeed" adds a stronger point that supports the first.

sentences: The new library is very popular.
It is often full by noon.
drills.hint: Use a semicolon before "indeed" and a comma after it.

sentences: Exercise is important for older people.
It can prevent many illnesses.
drills.hint: "Indeed" introduces evidence that makes the first claim stronger.

sentences: Tourism is vital to the island.
Most jobs depend on it.
drills.hint: The second clause confirms and strengthens the first.

sentences: Some species are under serious threat.
A few may disappear within decades.
drills.hint: "Indeed" moves from a general claim to a more serious one.

sentences: Traffic is a serious problem.
It may be the city's biggest challenge.
drills.hint: Build up the point: serious, and then even more serious after "indeed".

sentences: Many people think recycling is difficult.
It is actually quite simple.
drills.hint: "In fact" can correct a common belief.

sentences: Electric cars are not new.
They existed over a century ago.
drills.hint: Use "in fact" to add a surprising detail that proves the point.

sentences: The town's population has not fallen.
It has grown slightly.
drills.hint: "In fact" adds information that goes further than the first statement.

sentences: Too much homework is not always helpful.
It can reduce motivation.
drills.hint: The second clause makes the first point stronger, so use "in fact".

sentences: Breakfast is not essential for everyone.
Some people perform better without it.
drills.hint: Semicolon before, comma after "in fact".

sentences: The scheme was meant to save money.
It actually cost more than expected.
drills.hint: "But in fact" shows that the reality was different from the plan.

sentences: In the survey, several sports gained fans.
Tennis and cycling grew the most.
drills.hint: "Notably" picks out the most important examples, after a comma.

sentences: The school has improved in many areas.
Its science results show this most clearly.
drills.hint: Use "notably" + a phrase to highlight the clearest case.

sentences: Some foods are rich in protein.
Eggs and lentils are good examples.
drills.hint: "Notably" + examples can go between commas after the subject.

sentences: Many inventions came about by accident.
Penicillin is the best-known one.
drills.hint: Put the most famous example after "notably" at the end.

sentences: The region has changed greatly.
Its transport links have improved most.
drills.hint: "Notably" introduces the area of greatest change.

sentences: The film received several awards.
One of them was for its music.
drills.hint: "One" after "notably" refers back to one of the awards.

sentences: Parents should support their children.
Listening to them is most important.
drills.hint: "Above all" introduces the most important point.

sentences: A good diet should be varied.
Being balanced matters most.
drills.hint: Here "above all" sits between commas after "and".

sentences: Employers value many skills.
They look for good communication most of all.
drills.hint: After a semicolon, "above all" with a comma introduces the top priority.

sentences: Visitors want clean beaches.
Most of all, they want safe streets.
drills.hint: Put "above all" between commas before the most important item.

sentences: Teachers need many qualities.
Patience is the most important one.
drills.hint: "But above all" moves from many things to the single most important one.

sentences: The new policy aims to cut costs.
Its main aim is to protect jobs.
drills.hint: The two aims share one verb; "above all" marks the more important one.

sentences: The internet has changed how people shop.
There is no doubt about this.
drills.hint: A sentence adverb at the start shows certainty; it takes a comma.

sentences: Smartphones are certainly useful.
However, they can be addictive.
drills.hint: Admit the strong point first with certainty, then add the problem.

sentences: Climate change is a serious threat to many species.
Few scientists doubt this.
drills.hint: Use the adverb at the start when experts agree on a point.

sentences: Education is the key to development.
This is beyond doubt.
drills.hint: The adverb can sit between commas after "is".

sentences: Overall sales rose last year.
Online sales more than doubled.
drills.hint: As a sentence adverb, "significantly" marks an important detail.

sentences: Crime fell in the city last year.
Youth crime fell the most.
answer: fell in the city last year;
drills.hint: Use a semicolon, then the adverb and a comma to highlight the key finding.

sentences: The new teaching method helped all students.
Weaker students improved the most.
drills.hint: The adverb draws attention to the most important result.

sentences: Many people now work from home.
Most report being more productive.
drills.hint: "Significantly" signals that the next fact matters a lot.

sentences: The new park opened in spring.
Local air quality has improved since then.
drills.hint: Put the adverb after the semicolon and follow it with a comma.

sentences: The drug reduced symptoms.
It also caused very few side effects.
drills.hint: The adverb can sit between commas after "and" to stress the second result.

sentences: Online courses are flexible.
They require strong self-discipline.
drills.hint: This phrase draws attention to an important point; "that" is followed by a clause.

sentences: The survey shows rising satisfaction.
Only 200 people took part.
drills.hint: Use the phrase to point out a limitation of the evidence.

sentences: Nuclear power produces little carbon.
Its waste stays dangerous for centuries.
drills.hint: After "but", the phrase introduces a point the reader must not forget.

sentences: Prices have fallen recently.
The fall applies only to basic goods.
drills.hint: The phrase can open a sentence; it is followed by a full clause.
